desc:
A sequence is bitonic if it strictly increases up to some element (the peak) and then strictly decreases after it. Either side may be empty, so a strictly increasing sequence, a strictly decreasing sequence and a single element are all bitonic.

Return the length of the longest bitonic subsequence of nums (elements keep their original order but may be skipped). For nums = [1, 11, 2, 10, 4, 5, 2, 1] the answer is 6 (1, 2, 10, 5, 2, 1).
hints: Fix the peak at index i. The bitonic subsequence then splits into an increasing part ending at i and a decreasing part starting at i.
Compute inc[i], the longest strictly increasing subsequence ending at i, and dec[i], the longest strictly decreasing subsequence starting at i. The two parts only share the peak element.
The answer is the maximum of inc[i] + dec[i] - 1. Both arrays come from LIS in O(n log n): inc by a left-to-right pass, dec by running the same pass on the reversed array.
editorial: Every bitonic subsequence has a peak, and once the peak at index i is fixed the two sides are independent: the left side is a strictly increasing subsequence ending at i, the right side a strictly decreasing subsequence starting at i. Their best lengths are inc[i] and dec[i]; the peak is counted in both, so the best bitonic subsequence with peak i has length inc[i] + dec[i] - 1.

To compute inc use the tails technique: keep a sorted list of smallest tail values per length, and for each x find the slot with bisect_left; the slot index plus one is the length of the longest increasing subsequence ending at x. For dec, a decreasing subsequence starting at i is an increasing subsequence ending at i when you read the array from right to left, so run the same procedure on the reversed array and flip the result back.
Two O(n log n) passes plus a linear scan: O(n log n) time and O(n) space. The O(n<sup>2</sup>) DP with two nested loops is also fine for n = 5,000 in compiled languages.
